lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
Date of birth: 3 Mar 1997 | Nationality: Canadian
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Cut the card-dispute form's abandonment rate from 37% to 22% in a four-week A/B test by splitting it into three short steps with saved progress.
- Brought the design system to WCAG 2.1 AA by setting body-text contrast to at least 3:1 against every background.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Presented quarterly findings to the head of product and two design teams; three of the top five recommended fixes shipped in the next release cycle.
- Trained 12 product managers to run their own unmoderated tests with a shared script template, which doubled the number of tests run each quarter.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Jul 2019 - Feb 2022
- Raised the patient app's Net Promoter Score from 6.1 to 8.4, calculated as the average 0-10 recommendation rating across 2,000 monthly survey responses.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Writes the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Redesigned a city transit map for screen-reader and low-vision riders, and tested it with 12 participants on timed route-finding tasks.
- Cut median route-finding time from 90 to 60 seconds, a 50% improvement, by adding audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA), Tableau
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interveiws, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: Date of birth and nationality are included in the file.
items.because: They are not relevant to assessing the UX research experience and ask the reader to weigh personal information.

items.says: Education appears before Experience, so the UX research career does not lead the résumé.
items.because: The work history is the clearest evidence of the candidate’s UX research experience.

items.says: The A/B-test result does not identify whether the rates are control and variant or before and after.
items.because: A reader cannot tell how the A/B test supports the reported reduction.

items.says: A 3:1 contrast ratio does not meet WCAG 2.1 AA for ordinary-size body text.
items.because: Ordinary-size text requires at least 4.5:1; 3:1 applies only to qualifying large text.

items.says: The claim of bringing the whole design system to AA is broader than the stated body-text change.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the work covered the design system or only body-text contrast.

items.says: The sentence delays its 23% result behind a dense list of research inputs and methods.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the outcome.

items.says: “Synthesizing” leaves the sentence without a clear subject for the past-tense result.
items.because: The present participle and past-tense “cut” make it unclear who performed the action.

items.says: The sign-up result comes after the research methods instead of leading the bullet.
items.because: Moving the key outcome forward would make the impact easier to spot.

items.says: The bullet calls an average recommendation rating Net Promoter Score.
items.because: NPS is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors, not an average rating.

items.says: The result does not say what work drove the score change.
items.because: Without that link, the research skill behind the result is hard to assess.

items.says: The explanation of the rating measure is lengthy and slows scanning after the result.
The missed-appointment rates lack the period or population used for comparison.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the rates compare similar groups over comparable periods.

items.says: This strongest line in the entry does not open it.
items.because: It connects patient interviews to a product change and a measurable outcome.

items.says: “Writes” uses present tense for a role that ended in February 2022.
items.because: The inconsistency may leave a reader unsure whether the work continued.

items.says: The support-call reduction lacks a comparison period or basis.
items.because: A reader cannot judge whether it reflects comparable periods before and after the layout change.

items.says: The redesign line gives its audience and testing method but not what the redesign achieved.
items.because: It does not say what became easier or more accessible.

items.says: The sample size is repeated in the task-success bullet.
The time reduction is 33.3%, not 50%.
items.because: The 30-second decrease is one-third of the original 90 seconds.

items.says: The route-finding time result is not placed before the other project bullets.
items.because: Putting this concrete outcome first would make its impact easier to notice.

items.says: The audio-landmark and color method is repeated in the next result bullet.
The change is 20 percentage points, not 20%.
items.because: The endpoints differ by 20 percentage points; a 20% relative increase from 65% would produce 78%.

items.says: The participant count and method repeat details from the preceding bullets.
The booking-flow result does not say what design change you made or how you arrived at it.
items.because: A reader can see the outcome but not the UX skill behind the redesign.

items.says: The phone-booking reduction does not name the period it is compared with.
items.because: The line gives a time window but not the baseline period for the 25% figure.

items.says: “Hallway testing” is UX jargon that may not be clear outside the field.
“For maintaining the booking pages” is wordier than needed to describe the handbook’s purpose.
“interveiws” is misspelled in the Methods skills line.
items.because: The visible typo can distract from the methods being listed.
